A beginner can work in layers: the upper strings carry the melody, the lower strings the harmony, and the two strings off the fingerboard provide a drone, usually tuned an octave apart. When accompanying a singer the pitch can be above the singer's, and in practice you have to watch the range and the balance of the harmony.

Because it is bowed, its timbre has both the song of a string instrument and the continuity of a wind instrument. Compared with the sharpness and brilliance of the modern violin its timbre is more inward and deep; compared with the harp it is more dynamic. This distinctive tone made it an ideal choice for chamber music and accompaniment in the Renaissance.
臂琴於十五至十六世紀見於義大利宮廷，供詩人音樂家伴奏即興吟誦抒情與敘事詩。一五三: The lira da braccio appears in Italian courts in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, where poet-musicians used it to accompany improvised recitation of lyric and narrative poetry. It was first described in 1533 by Lanfranco, who also described its tuning. It rose with Petrarchan humanist verse and was popular in the northern Italian city states of Florence, Ferrara, Mantua and Venice. After the 1530s the rise of the madrigal, of instrumental consorts and of the violin pushed it back to festive stages or early continuo ensembles. The Pesaro manuscript preserves a dance intabulation for it; later a bass instrument, the lirone, was developed in turn.

The neck is mostly of plane or birch, giving structural stability. The strings are gut or early metal strings. The bridge is carved from maple, and the fine tuners and pegs are decorated with ivory or ebony, the whole showing the craftsmanship and the aesthetic aims of the Renaissance.

Its range is wide, covering the baritone to the treble, and the colour changes with the position on the fingerboard. The low register is warm and deep, the middle full and soft, the high clear and transparent.

The lira da Braccio is a European Renaissance bowed string instrument, a chordophone, Hornbostel-Sachs number 321.322-71, from Europe / Italy. It is closest to the medieval vielle, and looks roughly like a violin, but has a wider fingerboard, a flatter bridge and a leaf-shaped pegbox with the pegs facing forward. It usually has seven strings, five tuned like a violin plus one lower string, and two more outside the fingerboard as octave drones. Though its name refers to the arm, it is actually held on the shoulder and played with a long, strongly curved bow, which suits chords and three- and four-part harmony. Fifteenth- and sixteenth-century Italian court poet-musicians used it to accompany improvised recitation of lyric and narrative poetry, and it was occasionally used in intermedio ensembles, and may have had a proto-continuo role.
